title: One hundred and thirty-three years, 29 moments
lede: From a pharmacy in Atlanta to a vending machine in New York. Filter by thread.

events.title: The first glass
events.text: John Pemberton sells the first glass of Coca-Cola for a nickel at an Atlanta pharmacy soda fountain. First-year revenues are $35.

events.title: A new taste, found by accident
events.text: Company officials later say researchers came across the formula while working on Diet Coke.

events.title: The tests
events.text: Nearly 200,000 consumers are asked to compare formulas over a three-year period, by Time’s account. The new one wins 55–45 blind.

events.title: 21.7% to 18.8%
events.text: Coke’s share of the US soft drink market against Pepsi’s, per Beverage Digest figures quoted in July 1985. Coca-Cola’s sales for the year are $7.4 billion and its profit $629 million.

events.title: A “momentous announcement” is promised
events.text: Coca-Cola will not say what it is. Speculation centers on a smoother, sweeter formula.

events.title: The formula changes
events.text: In New York, Coca-Cola introduces the first major change to the formula in 99 years. The new drink goes on sale and production of the old one ends.

events.title: Pepsi takes a holiday
events.text: Pepsi declares a company holiday and Roger Enrico’s advertisement says “the other guy just blinked.”

events.title: Protest in Atlanta
events.text: Demonstrators at a Coca-Cola event downtown carry signs reading “We want the real thing.”

events.title: Overtime on the hotline
events.text: Employees are asked to volunteer for extra shifts. Company advertisements claim more than 80 million people have tried the new taste.

events.title: Pepsi’s best month
events.text: Pepsi advertisements say May sales were up 14%, the highest for any month in its history.

events.title: 1,500 calls a day
events.text: Brian Dyson says most are negative, and that 110 million people have tried the drink.

events.title: The old formula will return
events.text: Coca-Cola announces Coca-Cola Classic, to be sold beside the new Coke. Its stock rises $2.37.

events.title: The press conference
events.text: Goizueta and Keough explain the decision in Atlanta. The hotline takes 31,600 calls in two days.

events.title: Production of the original resumes
events.text: UPI reports from Washington state, where Gay Mullins celebrates.

events.title: The sugar lobby joins in
events.text: The Sugar Association runs full-page advertisements arguing that Classic, sweetened with corn syrup, is not the original either.

events.title: Two Cokes split the vote
events.text: By one later account, year-end surveys showed Pepsi ahead of the two Cokes; the new formula settled near 3%.

events.title: Classic retakes first place
events.text: The same account says Classic reclaimed the lead among sugar colas early in the year.

events.title: The centennial
events.text: Coca-Cola’s stock has gone from an all-time high of $74.75 to more than $115 since the reversal. Keough: “It all kind of worked out.”

events.title: About 39% to about 29%
events.text: Company shares of the soft drink market for Coca-Cola and PepsiCo, as the FTC moves to block their bids for Dr Pepper and Seven-Up.

events.title: A record year
events.text: Coca-Cola reports 1986 net income of $934 million, up 29%, and a domestic share above 39%.

events.title: A new name is announced
events.text: Coca-Cola says it will test-market the 1985 formula as Coke II later in the year.

events.title: Coke II reaches Spokane
events.text: Same taste, new packaging and advertising, on test in northeastern Washington and northern Idaho.

events.title: Classic 19.4%, Pepsi 17.3%
events.text: Brand shares for 1990 as reported by Beverage Industry magazine. The report does not list the new formula.

events.title: Coke II spreads, a little
events.text: Later accounts date the wider use of the Coke II name to 1992. We found no contemporary report we could open.

events.title: A tenth-anniversary party
events.text: Goizueta tells employees the decision was an example of “taking intelligent risks.”

events.title: Down to 0.1%
events.text: Snopes writes that the drink, now Coke II, “holds onto a 0.1% market share.”

events.title: Withdrawn
events.text: Two later accounts give 2002 as the end of Coke II. The Associated Press gives 2004.

events.title: “Classic” comes off the label
events.text: A spokesman says the reason for the word “has all but disappeared.” Canada had dropped it in 2007.

events.title: Back for “Stranger Things”
events.text: Coca-Cola and Netflix announce a limited run of New Coke cans, on sale from May 23 and dispensed free from pop-up vending machines.
